Learning no faster than the truth arrives

What it takes to build AI that improves itself, safely, inside a pharmaceutical launch.

Suyash Mishra, independent researcher, Zürich. September 2026.

Try the lag law

A loop corrects its error each week using an outcome that arrives several weeks late. Set how late the truth arrives, then how hard the loop reacts.

fastest unstable

The loop is ε(t+1) = ε(t) − k·ε(t − ℓ). It is stable only while k stays below 2·sin(π / (2(2ℓ + 1))), and it learns fastest, without overshoot, at k = ℓ^ℓ / (ℓ + 1)^(ℓ + 1).

A self-improving AI system in a drug launch is a feedback loop acting on a market whose truth arrives late. Whether it helps or harms depends less on how clever it is than on whether that loop is stable.

A launch is a feedback problem

About two-thirds of new medicines miss their first-year sales consensus, and most never recover. The trajectory is largely set within six months: launches that reach target prescriber breadth, repeat writing and depth by month six are about nine times more likely to succeed. The window in which intelligence can change the outcome is short.

Launch-intelligence platforms have converged on a familiar stack: a data foundation, a semantic layer, agents, scenario simulation, intelligence models, decision orchestration and a cockpit. What none of them does is improve itself. When a forecast misses or an agent misreads a payer document, people diagnose, fix, validate and release.

Across two papers and an open software package, I asked one question: can a launch-intelligence system improve itself, safely, inside a regulated market? The answer is yes, with conditions. You have to treat it as what it is: a system that learns from its own mistakes, on a market that tells you about those mistakes weeks, months or years later.

Why self-improving systems fail in a launch

Every self-improving system optimises what it can measure. In a launch, what you can measure fast is rarely what matters. Engagement, clicks and share of voice arrive in hours; new-to-brand prescriptions in weeks; formulary and HTA decisions in months; appropriately treated, persistent patients in quarters.

The long paper calls the slow, real outcomes anchors and ranks them by legitimacy: how directly they reflect patients, and how hard they are to move without moving patients. Engagement is a proxy that may inform but never decide. Prescriptions measured against a territory holdout can adjudicate a next-best-action loop. Persistent, appropriately treated patients adjudicate the system's revisions of itself.

The ranking has a consequence that shapes everything else: legitimacy rises with lag. A system that learns quickly learns from the signals easiest to game. A system that learns from the right signals must learn slowly. The recursive self-improvement literature has already documented systems that raised their own scores by disabling the checks meant to catch them; in a regulated market, that failure mode is not academic.

Not every decision should be learned by a machine

The long paper inventories 22 launch decisions, from evidence extraction and medical-legal pre-checks to price corridors and indication sequencing, and sorts them into three zones.

Zone (i): self-improvable

Content variants after MLR approval, next-best-action, evidence extraction, payer-document intelligence. The system may change these itself, under verification.

Zone (ii): simulator-mediated

Field allocation, persistence programmes, congress plans. The system may change these only through a scenario simulator that has proven its calibration.

Zone (iii): decision support only

Price corridor, launch sequence, positioning, indication sequencing, HTA submission. People decide; the engine supplies analysis and a regret frontier.

The short paper derives this boundary instead of asserting it. A loop whose truth arrives with lag ℓ can remove at most about 1 − e−(H/ℓ − 1) of its error within a window H, and none if ℓ ≥ H. With a six-month launch window, decisions anchored within about six weeks are learnable in time; decisions anchored beyond the window are not, however capable the model. Derived this way, the zoning agrees with the judgement-based version on 20 of 22 decisions.

Irreversibility adds a second, independent reason. A net price committed in one market lowers the reference-price ceiling in the markets that reference it, and that spillover cannot be undone. Price, sequence and positioning stay with people by construction, not by caution.

A self-improving system is a feedback system

Every launch team knows the bullwhip. A slow month of prescriptions prompts a cut in field effort; the cut shows up two months later, prompting a reversal; the reversal overshoots. Decision makers who act on lagged signals, and ignore effects already in flight, turn a stable system into an oscillating one.

A self-improving AI is the same decision maker, faster.

So the design question is not how clever the system's proposals are, but whether its loops are stable. The short paper derives seven stability laws in closed form. Four govern single loops; three govern systems of agents.

Laws for one loop
1
Lag lawLearn no faster than the truth arrives.

A loop learning at rate k from truth with lag ℓ is stable only if kℓ < π/2, and learns fastest, without overshoot, at kℓ = 1/e. Above that, over-reaction is not just riskier but slower. At the boundary the loop rings with a period of about four lags: the bullwhip, quantified.

2
Refresh lawRe-anchor a proxy faster than it is exploited.

An evaluator's bias grows without bound unless it is re-fitted against real outcomes. Re-fitting it on its own scores resets the clock, not the bias.

3
Separation lawKeep the judge slower than the judged.

A verifier acting on stale evidence cycles with the proposer it checks. A verifier frozen within an epoch and re-anchored at its boundary converges.

4
Ladder lawChange yourself only by more than you can mismeasure.

Inherit a revision only when its measured gain exceeds the measurement error, and report only the uncertainty you can keep calibrated.

Laws for many agents
5
Coupling lawTune agents to the market they share.

Two agents reaching the same prescribers, each stable alone, can be unstable together. Gains must be set from the largest eigenvalue of their interaction; agents working against each other are unstable at any gain.

6
Constraint lawShield what you can check.

Legal limits and price corridors are removed before anything is scored, so they are never breached and never learned. A constraint observed only afterwards, like a payer budget, is a feedback loop, and its multiplier obeys the lag law.

7
Connectivity lawEvery hop spends margin.

A human review gate, a protocol hop and a batch each add to a loop's lag. Review turnaround is not free of dynamics; it is delay, and delay is what the lag law charges for.

Each law was tested against simulation rather than assumed. The stability and no-overshoot boundaries matched within the 5% grid resolution. The critical verifier delay was predicted and observed at exactly seven rounds. Coupled agents lost stability at exactly the predicted strength. A stability monitor measured a loop's effective lag at 4.09 weeks against a predicted 4.1, damped its gain, and cut the oscillation from 0.85 to 0.02.

Seven agents and one pricing decision

The hardest test is a decision the thesis says machines should not make. The PR-01 decision record asks: what is the global value-based price aspiration, and what evidence anchors it? The accountable owner is Global Pricing with Local Pricing & Access. Agents may support and recommend, nothing more.

The software package compiles that record directly into a system. Each required-evidence item becomes an agent reading its source through a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server: value evidence, reference pricing, local willingness-to-pay, access and volume, gross-to-net, competitor landscape, legal constraints. Agents send evidence to each other as Agent2Agent (A2A) messages carrying a governance envelope: scope, model family, evaluator epoch, provenance hash, capability token and budget. The owner decides through an A2A task, and a hash-chained ledger records every tool call, message, decision and anchor.

The decision contract sets every parameter: gains, dual steps and margins come from the laws, not from tuning. Over a stylised ten-market launch with reference-price spillover, 200 paired runs compared the governed agents with a single local analysis built on the affiliate's willingness-to-pay study, scored on the contract's own objective of portfolio value and sustainable access.

Values are shares of an oracle that knows the true market parameters.

When the local study is strong, one good analyst is better, and significantly so. The governed agents' value is resilience: as the local study weakens, they lose 1.8 points where the single analysis loses 6.8.

Three further results matter as much as the table:

  • The governed agents improve themselves. With a weak local study, their regret falls from 0.089 in the first market to 0.035 in the tenth, as anchors teach them how competitor prices and payer budgets relate to willingness-to-pay.
  • The same agents with the laws violated get worse as they learn. Their regret rises from 0.184 to 0.232. They average 3.4 hard-constraint breaches per launch against zero, and their intervals cover reality 29% of the time against 93%.
  • Agents that post conclusions instead of likelihoods are worse than one good analyst at every level of evidence. What agents send each other is a first-order design decision.

What building it taught us

The most useful part of this work was the part that went wrong. Five errors surfaced only when the decision record ran end to end, and each was found by isolating a component against theory, not by tuning until the numbers looked good.

  • Score on the contract's objective. An early run scored everything on value alone. The contract asks for value and sustainable access; the governed agents were buying access and being penalised for honouring the contract.
  • Exchange likelihoods, not conclusions. Competitor prices and the payer budget per patient both carry information about willingness-to-pay. When each agent posted its own conclusion, the synthesis hedged over roughly twice the uncertainty the combined evidence supports. Agents now send a likelihood and the structural link they learned, and the synthesis fuses them.
  • The lag law governs closed loops only. Estimating something the system does not influence, such as population willingness-to-pay, has no feedback through the delay. Its learning rate should come from statistics, not stability. I had misapplied my own law, and the correction is now part of the theory.
  • Calibrate against the anchor's own noise. The negotiated price that reveals willingness-to-pay is itself noisy; checking intervals against it inflated every interval until the calibration target was corrected.
  • A wrong prior is expensive. Pooling toward a value-evidence prior that was 22% low cost about five points. The prior is itself something to anchor and refresh.

The long paper keeps a public record of its own corrections too. An early headline overstated one ratio, which in fact ranges from 1.5× to 7.9× depending on how gameable the proxy is. An alignment threshold was set low enough that a misspecified objective would have passed it. And an earlier pricing study's mean advantage turned out not to be statistically significant. Each correction made the claims smaller and the work more trustworthy.

The finding that matters most

The speed of safe self-improvement is set by how precisely a system can measure itself. Improving the proposer does far less.

The ladder law makes a system inherit a change to itself only when the measured gain clearly exceeds its measurement error. That rule is safe but slow. In simulation, with realistic measurement noise, a system obeying it gained 0.04 in true yield over 40 revision cycles. Halving the noise, roughly four times the evaluation data, raised that to 0.30. Halving it again raised it to 0.76: twenty times faster, with the chance of ever inheriting a harmful change below 0.6% throughout.

A greedy system that inherits whatever looks better did gain more, 0.62, but inherited nine to ten harmful changes and claimed 2.6 times the improvement it actually delivered. It was improving, and deceiving itself about how much.

This is why the long paper puts an evaluation instrument at the centre of the design rather than at the end. The instrument looks at every result through five lenses: counterfactual (against a holdout or the incumbent replayed), temporal (drift, and whether early signals can be trusted), comparative, causal (which funnel transition moved) and adaptive. The adaptive lens checks whether the objective itself is right. When measured progress stops tracking brand value, it proposes revised objective weights for people to ratify. In simulation it caught a misspecified, engagement-heavy objective at the first review and recovered 59% of the value gap.

What this means if you run launches

None of this requires a new model. It requires writing things down that launch organisations mostly keep in people's heads, and treating time as a design variable.

  • Write decisions as contracts. Question, accountable owner, authority boundary, required evidence, valid options, decision rule, monitoring. A contract like PR-01 compiles into agents whose parameters can be inspected.
  • Map your anchors per market. For each signal, record its source, its lag, how legitimate it is, and whether anyone in the loop can write to it. A number a launch team can edit is a proxy.
  • Start where the truth is fast. Content after MLR approval, next-best-action, evidence extraction and payer-document intelligence are learnable inside the launch window. Price is not.
  • Count review time as delay. Route to human review by impact, not habit, and set each loop's learning rate at its effective lag, including the review turnaround.
  • Tune agents that share prescribers or budgets together. Two well-behaved agents can oscillate once they act on the same people.
  • Put the money into measurement. Larger holdouts, cleaner pairing and faster, cleaner anchors buy more safe improvement than a smarter model.
  • Keep price, sequencing and positioning with people, and give those people a regret frontier across scenarios instead of a point recommendation.

The first real test should be small and pre-registered. The companion protocol specifies one: a matched-pair territory holdout of one next-best-action template in one market, with weekly new-to-brand prescriptions as the anchor. It runs an eight-week baseline and eight weeks of treatment, needs about 39 territory pairs to detect a 4% lift, and defines in advance what a pass, a null and a guardrail breach would each mean.

What this does not claim

Every result here is simulated. The launch environment is stylised and not calibrated to any real market; the human owner is simulated; the laws are local and linear, while real agents include language models, people and markets. The work establishes that the design is coherent, that its laws hold where they are supposed to, and that a real pricing decision can be executed within them. It does not establish that any of this works on a real launch. That is what the field protocol is for.

What I hope it does establish is a way of thinking. A self-improving system is safe to the extent that it is stable. It is stable to the extent that it learns no faster than the truth arrives, re-anchors what it is tempted to game, keeps its judges slower than what they judge, changes itself only by more than it can mismeasure, tunes agents to the market they share, shields what it can check, and counts every gate and hop as delay. In a launch, those rules decide which decisions a machine may learn in the six months that matter, and which it must leave to the people accountable for them.
